title: Your Critical Role in Troubling Times: What you say—and how you say it—matters
author: Kurt Mueller
summary: Prompted by a client facing federal layoffs, Mueller argues that in uncertainty leaders must fill the information vacuum or fear and speculation will. He sets out three do-not and do-instead pairs: offer transparency rather than false assurances, commit to scheduled updates rather than saying you will tell them if anything changes, and show emotional steadiness rather than transmitting anger or helplessness. Each comes with sample wording leaders can adapt. The latter half lists adjacent capabilities and a four-step Pause, Assess, Adapt, Act framework, and the piece promotes his coaching framework, but the communication guidance on honesty, cadence and composure is the substantive core.
points: Uncertainty creates an information vacuum that leaders must fill honestly or fear will fill it.
Empty reassurance erodes credibility; naming what you do and do not know builds it.
A scheduled update commitment, even when there is nothing new, beats vague promises to tell people if anything changes.
A leader's anger or helplessness transmits to the team, so regulate before engaging and keep discussion focused on what can be controlled.
quotes: Uncertainty creates an information vacuum, and when leaders don’t fill it, fear and speculation take over. People begin to make assumptions, often assuming the worst.

In times of uncertainty, leaders may feel tempted to reassure their teams with statements like "Everything will be fine" or "There’s nothing to worry about." However, when employees sense real risk—such as potential layoffs—empty reassurances can erode trust.

The best approach is to be honest about what you know and what you don’t, while reinforcing your commitment to keeping employees informed. A transparent message builds credibility and reassures people that they won’t be left in the dark.

Saying this can leave employees feeling uncertain and anxious. Without a clear expectation of when or how updates will come, the team is left guessing about the situation’s seriousness and when they might hear more. This can lead to speculation, distractions, and decreased morale.
Expressing anger, frustration, or helplessness as a leader doesn’t just reflect your emotions—it transmits them to the team.

Before engaging with your team, take a moment to regulate your emotions. Whether it’s through a quick reflection, deep breathing, or mentally preparing for the discussion, your ability to remain composed sets the tone for the group.
This response acknowledges emotions without amplifying them and shifts the focus toward productive action.
